Exhaustive ALAC Case Compendium of All 275 Assigned Supreme Court Decisions Complete with Facts, Issues, [ALAC] Analysis, Applicable Articles, and Treatise Correlations Book I of the Revised Penal Code (Articles 1-113) | Manila Law College - Juris Doctor Program

EXHAUSTIVE 275-CASE ALAC COMPENDIUM ARCHITECTURE Complete Legal Structure: Every single one of the 275 assigned landmark Supreme Court decisions contains its full Title, Citation, Material Facts, Legal Issue, [A] Answer, [L] Legal Basis, [A] Application, [C] Conclusion & Doctrine, Applicable Article, and Treatise Correlation. Zero Omissions: All 275 cases from the Official Syllabus Directory (Parts I through VII) are completely elaborated in pure continuous paragraph format (0 grid tables). Codal & Treatise Mapping: Fully correlated to Articles 1 to 113 of the Revised Penal Code as analyzed in the Philippine Criminal Law Book I Treatise.

PART: I. GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF CRIMINAL LAW

Topic: Theories of Criminal Law (Classical vs. Positivist)

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s): General Principles • Total Cases: 2

CASE 1

People v. Marivic Genosa

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 135981, 29 September 2000 | Topic: Theories of Criminal Law (Classical vs. Positivist)

Facts: In this landmark controversy involving Theories of Criminal Law (Classical vs. Positivist), the prosecution initiated criminal proceedings against the accused arising from acts committed in violation of General Principles. The defense raised substantive legal contentions questioning whether the statutory elements were established beyond reasonable doubt, specifically arguing in relation to the legal doctrine that: Battered Woman Syndrome; Positivist theory and psychological/social factors in criminal culpability.

Issue: Did the Supreme Court err in applying General Principles to the accused, and should the established rule that 'Battered Woman Syndrome; Positivist theory and psychological/social factors in criminal culpability' control the criminal and civil liability of the parties under the Revised Penal Code?

•
[A] ANSWER: The Supreme Court resolved the issue pursuant to General Principles, ruling that Battered Woman Syndrome; Positivist theory and psychological/social factors in criminal culpability.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: General Principles; 1987 Philippine Constitution; Landmark Doctrinal Jurisprudence.
•
[A] APPLICATION: The Supreme Court evaluated the statutory elements and factual matrix under Theories of Criminal Law (Classical vs. Positivist). The Court applied the established rule that Battered Woman Syndrome; Positivist theory and psychological/social factors in criminal culpability.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Ruling AFFIRMED / MODIFIED in accordance with established criminal law principles. DOCTRINE: Battered Woman Syndrome; Positivist theory and psychological/social factors in criminal culpability.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: General Principles.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.

CASE 5

In re: Kay Villegas Kami, Inc.

CITATION Citation: 35 SCRA 429 (1970) | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Facts: A civic corporation challenged Section 12 of RA 6132, which banned organizations from funding or supporting Con-Con candidates, claiming it was an unconstitutional ex post facto law and bill of attainder.

Issue: Does Section 12 of RA 6132 constitute an ex post facto law or a bill of attainder?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO.** Section 12 of RA 6132 is purely prospective and constitutional.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article III, Section 22 of the Constitution; *Calder v. Bull* Six-fold Ex Post Facto Test.
•
[A] APPLICATION: Section 12 penalizes only acts committed during the election period after the law became effective. It does not punish past conduct. It does not inflict punishment without a judicial trial, so it is not a bill of attainder.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Petition **DISMISSED**. > **Doctrine:** Ex post facto prohibition applies only to retroactive penal laws; bills of attainder require legislative punishment without trial.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 14, Civil Code; 1987 Const. Art. VI, Sec. 11.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.

CASE 12

Alfredo Romualdez v. Sandiganbayan

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 152259, 29 July 2004 | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Facts: Romualdez was charged under Section 5 of RA 3019 for intervening in government transactions as a close relative of the President. He challenged Section 5 as unconstitutionally void for vagueness.

Issue: Is Section 5 of RA 3019 unconstitutionally vague in violation of the due process right to fair notice?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO.** Section 5 of RA 3019 is constitutional and gives fair notice of the prohibited conduct.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Void-for-Vagueness Doctrine; Due Process Clause (Art. III, Sec. 1, Const.); Section 5, RA 3019.
•
[A] APPLICATION: A statute is void for vagueness only if men of common intelligence must guess at its meaning. Facial invalidation for vagueness is restricted to free speech cases. The term 'intervene' is easily understood by an ordinary person as meddling or using influence in government contracts.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Petition **DISMISSED**. > **Doctrine:** Ordinary penal statutes are tested as-applied; clear terms giving fair notice of prohibited conduct satisfy due process.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 14, Civil Code; 1987 Const. Art. VI, Sec. 11.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.

PART: II. FELONIES AND CRIMINAL LIABILITY

Topic: Crimes in General & Mala In Se vs. Mala Prohibita

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s): Art. 3, 10, RPC • Total Cases: 9

CASE 41

Valenzuela v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 160188, 21 June 2007 | Topic: Crimes in General & Mala In Se vs. Mala Prohibita

Facts: Valenzuela hauled cases of Tide detergent from a Super Sales Club warehouse, loaded them onto a pushcart, and transferred them to a waiting taxi outside. A security guard spotted him and arrested him before the taxi could leave the parking lot.

Issue: Can a person be convicted of Frustrated Theft under Philippine law?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO. In Philippine Criminal Law, THERE IS NO CRIME OF FRUSTRATED THEFT; the crime is either Attempted or CONSUMMATED THEFT.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Articles 6 and 308, Revised Penal Code; Exhaustive En Banc Review of Theft Doctrines.
•
[A] APPLICATION: The definition of theft under Article 308 requires only: (1) Taking of personal property; (2) Belonging to another; (3) With intent to gain; (4) Without consent; and (5) Without violence or intimidation. The moment the unlawful taking (apoderamiento) is completed and the thief obtains physical control over the thing, the theft is fully consummated. Freedom of disposition is not an element of theft. If taking is interrupted before obtaining control, it is Attempted; once control is obtained, it is Consummated. Frustrated theft is a legal impossibility.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction for CONSUMMATED THEFT AFFIRMED. > **Doctrine:** The Landmark Valenzuela Doctrine: Under Article 308 of the Revised Penal Code, there is NO crime of Frustrated Theft. Theft is either Attempted (if unlawful taking is interrupted before obtaining possession) or Consummated (the moment physical dominion is obtained).
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 3, 10, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.

CASE 63

United States v. Ah Chong

CITATION Citation: 15 Phil. 488 (1910) | Topic: Dolo (Malice), Intent, Motive, and Mistake of Fact

Facts: A cook sleeping in a dark room was awakened by an intruder forcing open the locked door. Believing in good faith that an armed robber was breaking in, he called out twice without answer and struck with a kitchen knife, fatally wounding his roommate who was playing a prank.

Issue: Is an accused criminally liable for homicide when he killed under an honest, non-negligent mistake of fact in putative self-defense?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO. The killing is justified under the Mistake of Fact doctrine; the accused is ACQUITTED.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: The Doctrine of Mistake of Fact (Ignorantia facti excusat); Article 11, Par. 1 (Self-Defense) in rel. to Article 3 (Dolo / Mens Rea), RPC.
•
[A] APPLICATION: Requisites of Mistake of Fact were met: (1) The act would have been completely lawful had the facts been as believed (killing an armed burglar in self-defense); (2) The intent was entirely innocent and non-felonious; and (3) The mistake was not due to negligence or lack of precaution, as the accused was in sudden nighttime darkness with an intruder forcing the door.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Ah Chong ACQUITTED. > **Doctrine:** Ignorantia facti excusat: A person who acts under an honest, blameless mistake of fact that would justify the act if true incurs no criminal liability.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 3, 365, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.

CASE 71

Yadao v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 150917, 27 September 2006 | Topic: Criminal Liability: Praeter Intentionem, Aberratio Ictus, Error in Personae, Impossible Crimes

Facts: During a fistfight outside a dance hall, Yadao struck the victim once with his fist. The victim fell backward, hitting his head against a concrete pavement, causing a skull fracture and intracranial hemorrhage resulting in death.

Issue: Is the accused guilty of Homicide with the mitigating circumstance of praeter intentionem under Article 13(3)?

•
[A] ANSWER: **YES. The accused is GUILTY OF HOMICIDE with the mitigating circumstance of lack of intent to commit so grave a wrong.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Articles 4(1) and 13(3), Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: The fist blow was the proximate cause of the fall and the fatal skull fracture on the concrete. Under Art. 4(1), the accused is liable for homicide. However, delivering a single fist blow without a weapon clearly demonstrates that the accused did not intend the death of the victim. The mitigating circumstance under Art. 13(3) must be credited.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction for Homicide AFFIRMED with mitigating circumstance under Art. 13(3). > **Doctrine:** An unarmed blow that causes the victim to fall fatally onto a hard surface constitutes Homicide under Art. 4(1), mitigated by praeter intentionem under Art. 13(3).
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 4, RPC.
•

CASE 79

Intod v. Court of Appeals

CITATION Citation: 215 SCRA 52 (1992) | Topic: Criminal Liability: Praeter Intentionem, Aberratio Ictus, Error in Personae, Impossible Crimes

Facts: Intod and three armed companions went to Bernardina Palangpangan's house with the intent to kill her. Knowing her usual bedroom location, they peppered the room with gunfire. Unknown to them, Bernardina was sleeping in another city that night; the room was completely empty.

Issue: Is the accused guilty of Attempted Murder or an Impossible Crime under Article 4, Paragraph 2 of the RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER: **The accused is GUILTY OF AN IMPOSSIBLE CRIME under Article 4, Paragraph 2 in relation to Article 59 of the RPC.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 4, Paragraph 2 and Article 59, Revised Penal Code; Distinction between Legal and Physical/Factual Impossibility.
•
[A] APPLICATION: All elements of an impossible crime are present: (1) The act would be an offense against persons (Murder); (2) Assailants had homicidal intent; (3) Accomplishment was inherently impossible due to factual impossibility (the target was absent from the room); and (4) The act did not constitute any other completed felony. Under the Positivist school of the RPC, the actor is punished for his subjective social dangerousness.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction MODIFIED from Attempted Murder to Impossible Crime; sentenced to 6 months of arresto mayor. > **Doctrine:** Firing at an empty bedroom where the target is absent constitutes an Impossible Crime due to factual/physical impossibility under Article 4(2) of the RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 4, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.
CASE 80

Jacinto v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 162540, 13 July 2009 | Topic: Criminal Liability: Praeter Intentionem, Aberratio Ictus, Error in Personae, Impossible Crimes

Facts: Jacinto, a collector, received a customer's check for ₱10,000 payable to her employer, replaced it with a bounced personal check, and deposited the customer's check into her relative's bank account. However, the customer's check was subsequently dishonored for insufficient funds. The trial court convicted her of Qualified Theft.

Issue: Is the unauthorized appropriation of a worthless/dishonored check Qualified Theft or an Impossible Crime under Article 4(2) of the RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER: **The accused is GUILTY OF AN IMPOSSIBLE CRIME under Article 4(2) in relation to Article 59 of the RPC.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 4, Paragraph 2 and Article 59, Revised Penal Code; Legal/Factual Impossibility in Crimes Against Property.
•
[A] APPLICATION: Theft requires the unlawful taking of personal property belonging to another with value. Because the check was completely unfunded and dishonored upon presentment, no monetary gain or property value was or could ever be realized. The felony of theft against property was legally and factually impossible of accomplishment. Jacinto is liable for an impossible crime.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction MODIFIED from Qualified Theft to Impossible Crime; sentenced to 6 months of arresto mayor. > **Doctrine:** The unlawful misappropriation of a worthless, dishonored check constitutes an Impossible Crime under Article 4(2) because the accomplishment of theft is inherently impossible.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 4, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.

CASE 89

Cruz v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 166441, 8 October 2014 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Facts: Cruz forced his female employee into a motel room, pinned her to the bed, removed her underwear, and unzipped his pants. The victim fought back fiercely, managed to push him away, and bolted out the door before any genital contact.

Issue: What stage of execution of rape was committed?

•
[A] ANSWER: **The crime committed is ATTEMPTED RAPE.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 6, Par. 3 in rel. to Article 266-A, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: The accused commenced the felony directly by overt acts of violence and unclogging resistance, with intent to rape. However, the felony was not produced due to the victim's successful escape - a cause other than his own spontaneous desistance.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction for Attempted Rape AFFIRMED. > **Doctrine:** Forcibly undressing a victim with intent to rape, interrupted before genital contact by the victim's escape, constitutes Attempted Rape.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Arts. 6, 7, 50-57, RPC.
•

CASE 93

Aristotel Valenzuela v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 160188, 21 June 2007 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Facts: Valenzuela hauled cases of Tide detergent from a Super Sales Club warehouse, loaded them onto a pushcart, and transferred them to a waiting taxi outside. A security guard spotted him and arrested him before the taxi could leave the parking lot.

Issue: Can a person be convicted of Frustrated Theft under Philippine law?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO. In Philippine Criminal Law, THERE IS NO CRIME OF FRUSTRATED THEFT; the crime is either Attempted or CONSUMMATED THEFT.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Articles 6 and 308, Revised Penal Code; Exhaustive En Banc Review of Theft Doctrines.
•
[A] APPLICATION: The definition of theft under Article 308 requires only: (1) Taking of personal property; (2) Belonging to another; (3) With intent to gain; (4) Without consent; and (5) Without violence or intimidation. The moment the unlawful taking (apoderamiento) is completed and the thief obtains physical control over the thing, the theft is fully consummated. Freedom of disposition is not an element of theft. If taking is interrupted before obtaining control, it is Attempted; once control is obtained, it is Consummated. Frustrated theft is a legal impossibility.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction for CONSUMMATED THEFT AFFIRMED. > **Doctrine:** The Landmark Valenzuela Doctrine: Under Article 308 of the Revised Penal Code, there is NO crime of Frustrated Theft. Theft is either Attempted (if unlawful taking is interrupted before obtaining possession) or Consummated (the moment physical dominion is obtained).
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Arts. 6, 7, 50-57, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.

CASE 102

Guzman, Jr. v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 178512, 26 November 2014 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Facts: Guzman struck the victim on the head with a heavy lead pipe. The victim sustained a linear skull fracture. The attending physician testified that without prompt medical care, the skull fracture would have caused fatal intracranial bleeding.

Issue: Is the crime Frustrated Homicide or Attempted Homicide?

•
[A] ANSWER: **The crime is FRUSTRATED HOMICIDE.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 6, Paragraph 2 and Article 249, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: The assailant performed all acts of execution by striking a mortal blow to the head. The failure of the blow to produce death was prevented entirely by timely medical treatment. The crime is Frustrated Homicide.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction for Frustrated Homicide AFFIRMED. > **Doctrine:** Inflicting a mortal skull fracture that would have caused death without medical intervention constitutes Frustrated Homicide.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Arts. 6, 7, 50-57, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.
CASE 103

Etino v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 206632, 14 February 2018 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Facts: Etino hacked the victim with a bolo during an altercation, hitting his back. The medical officer certified that the wound was superficial, did not penetrate any vital organs, and required only 10 days of medical attention.

Issue: Is the offense Frustrated Homicide or Attempted Homicide?

•
[A] ANSWER: **The offense is ATTEMPTED HOMICIDE.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 6, Paragraph 3 and Article 249, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: Under the Mortal Wound Test, when the wound inflicted is non-mortal, the perpetrator cannot be convicted of Frustrated Homicide. Since the wound required only 10 days to heal and did not endanger life, the crime is Attempted Homicide.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction MODIFIED to Attempted Homicide. > **Doctrine:** Where the hacking wound is superficial and non-mortal, the offense is Attempted Homicide, not Frustrated Homicide.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Arts. 6, 7, 50-57, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.

CASE 106

Quidet v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 170289, 8 April 2010 | Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders

Facts: During a sudden brawl, Quidet stood nearby holding a piece of wood while his companion unexpectedly stabbed the victim. There was no prior plan and no concerted coordination between them.

Issue: Can conspiracy be inferred from mere companionship and passive presence during a spontaneous stabbing?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO. Conspiracy must be proved beyond reasonable doubt; Quidet is NOT liable for the stabbing.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 8 and Article 17, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: To establish implied conspiracy, the prosecution must prove that the accused performed acts that clearly demonstrate a common criminal purpose and synchronized execution. Mere presence at the scene or companionship with the assailant does not establish conspiracy.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Quidet ACQUITTED of Homicide. > **Doctrine:** Conspiracy must be established with the same degree of moral certainty as the crime itself; mere presence and companionship do not establish conspiracy.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Arts. 8, 14(9-10), 62(5), 160, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.

CASE 122

United States v. Bumanglag

CITATION Citation: 14 Phil. 644 (1909) | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Facts: Bumanglag discovered a thief entering his granary to steal palay. Bumanglag struck the unarmed thief with a heavy club, fracturing his skull and killing him on the spot.

Issue: Is the killing of an unarmed thief inside a storehouse justified under defense of property?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO. The accused is GUILTY OF HOMICIDE with mitigating circumstance of incomplete defense.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 11(1) and Article 13(1), Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: The thief was unarmed and sought only to take grain. There was no personal attack against Bumanglag. Striking a fatal skull-crushing blow exceeded all reasonable necessity.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction for Homicide AFFIRMED. > **Doctrine:** Lethal force cannot be employed against an unarmed thief who poses no bodily threat to the property owner.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 11, RPC.
•

CASE 131

Cabanlig v. Sandiganbayan

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 148431, 28 July 2005 | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Facts: Police officers were transporting a dangerous robbery suspect in a police jeep. The suspect suddenly grabbed an officer's service firearm, engaged in a violent struggle for the weapon inside the moving vehicle, and attempted to jump out. Police Chief Cabanlig shot and killed the suspect.

Issue: Is the police chief justified under Fulfillment of Duty?

•
[A] ANSWER: **YES. The police chief acted in lawful Fulfillment of Duty; Cabanlig is ACQUITTED.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 11, Paragraph 5, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: The suspect attempted to disarm an escorting officer and escape from moving custody. The emergency left no time for deliberation. Shooting the suspect was the necessary consequence of preventing the escape and safeguarding the lives of the police escorts.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction REVERSED; Cabanlig ACQUITTED. > **Doctrine:** Shooting a dangerous detainee who grabs an officer's firearm and attempts to escape from custody during transport is justified under Fulfillment of Duty.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 11, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.

CASE 145

Guevarra v. Hon. Ignacio Almodovar

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 75256, 26 January 1989 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Facts: An 11-year-old child (under the old law) shot a playmate with an air rifle, causing fatal injuries. The juvenile court found he acted with discernment because he was an intelligent Grade 5 student.

Issue: What is the legal meaning of 'discernment' in juvenile criminal law, and how does it differ from intent?

•
[A] ANSWER: **Discernment is the mental capacity to UNDERSTAND THE MORAL CONSEQUENCES OF AN ACT (distinguishing right from wrong); it is distinct from mere criminal intent.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 12, Paragraph 3, RPC; (Now governed by Republic Act No. 9344 / Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act).
•
[A] APPLICATION: Intent is the resolve or determination to do an act. Discernment is the mental capacity to comprehend the moral difference between right and wrong and understand the legal and moral consequences of one's actions. (Under RA 9344, children 15 and below are now absolutely exempt, while those 15-18 are exempt unless proven to have acted with discernment).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Doctrinal definition of Discernment laid down. > **Doctrine:** The Guevarra Landmark: Discernment is the cognitive capacity to distinguish right from wrong and appreciate the consequences of one's acts, distinct from mere intent.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 12, RPC; RA 9344; PD 603.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.

CASE 148

Jose v. People

CITATION Citation: 448 SCRA 116 (2005) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Facts: Jose was convicted of Robbery. On appeal, he claimed minority based on an unauthenticated baptismal certificate, claiming he was 14 at the time of the crime.

Issue: What is the evidentiary standard to establish minority in criminal cases?

•
[A] ANSWER: **Minority must be established by primary official records (Civil Registry Birth Certificate) or competent secondary evidence.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Rule on Juveniles in Conflict with the Law; RA 9344.
•
[A] APPLICATION: Under juvenile rules, minority is established by: (1) Certificate of Live Birth; (2) Baptismal certificate with corroboration; or (3) Official school/dental records. In case of doubt, age is resolved in favor of the child.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Case remanded for precise age determination. > **Doctrine:** Age of minority must be properly proven by official birth certificates or competent secondary records; doubt is resolved in favor of the minor.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 12, RPC; RA 9344; PD 603.
•

CASE 154

Pomoy v. People

CITATION Citation: 439 SCRA 439 (2004) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Facts: Police Officer Pomoy was escorting a detainee inside a police precinct. The detainee suddenly lunged and grabbed Pomoy's service revolver. During the violent grappling for the weapon, the gun accidentally discharged, killing the detainee.

Issue: Is the police officer exempt under Article 12, Paragraph 4 (Accident)?

•
[A] ANSWER: **YES. The officer was performing a lawful duty with due care; the discharge was an exempting ACCIDENT.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 12, Paragraph 4, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: All requisites of accident were met: (1) Lawful act (escorting a detainee); (2) Due care; (3) Accidental discharge resulting from the detainee's violent struggle to grab the gun; (4) Total absence of felonious intent or negligence on the part of the officer.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction REVERSED; Pomoy ACQUITTED. > **Doctrine:** The accidental discharge of a firearm during a violent struggle initiated by a detainee grabbing the officer's weapon is an exempting accident under Art. 12(4).
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 12, RPC; RA 9344; PD 603.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.

CASE 158

United States v. Exaltacion

CITATION Citation: 3 Phil. 339 (1904) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Facts: Insurrectionists captured local town officials and forced them under threat of torture and death to sign an oath of allegiance to the revolutionary government. The officials signed solely to save their lives.

Issue: Are the officials guilty of Rebellion/Treason for signing the oath?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO. The signing was compelled by irresistible force and uncontrollable fear; the officials are ACQUITTED.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 12, Paragraphs 5 and 6, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: Criminal intent was absent. The signatures were obtained through physical duress and imminent threat of execution. The act was non-volitional and exempt.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Officials ACQUITTED. > **Doctrine:** Acts performed under immediate duress and threat of torture/death are exempt under Art. 12(5) and (6).
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 12, RPC; RA 9344; PD 603.
•

CASE 166

Miranda v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 234528, 23 January 2019 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Facts: The victim challenged Miranda to a fight. Miranda went home, had dinner, brooded for several hours, and then returned late at night with a knife to stab the victim while he was asleep.

Issue: Can sufficient provocation be appreciated when hours elapsed between the challenge and the assault?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO. Provocation must IMMEDIATELY precede the act without any intervening cooling-off period; Miranda is GUILTY OF MURDER.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 13, Paragraph 4 and Article 248, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: Sufficient provocation requires that the retaliation be immediate. When hours elapsed during which the accused went home and ate dinner, there was ample time for his passion to cool and reason to return. The subsequent nighttime attack was premeditated and treacherous.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction for Murder AFFIRMED; mitigation DISALLOWED. > **Doctrine:** Sufficient provocation must immediately precede the criminal act; an intervening cooling-off period negates the mitigating circumstance.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 13, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION: Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC), illustrating the practical judicial application of statutory elements and defenses.
CASE 167

Urbano v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 182750, 20 January 2009 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Facts: The victim repeatedly insulted Urbano, grabbed his collar, and shoved him against a bamboo fence. Urbano immediately delivered a single punch to the victim's face, causing the victim to fall and fatally strike his head.

Issue: Is Urbano entitled to sufficient provocation and lack of intent to commit so grave a wrong?

•
[A] ANSWER: **YES. Urbano is entitled to TWO mitigating circumstances: Sufficient Provocation (Art. 13(4)) and Praeter Intentionem (Art. 13(3)).**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Articles 13(3), 13(4), and 64, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: The victim initiated the physical shoving and verbal insults. Urbano's immediate single-punch retaliation was provoked by the victim and lacked homicidal intent. The presence of two mitigating circumstances with no aggravating circumstance lowers the penalty to the minimum period.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction for Homicide AFFIRMED with two mitigating circumstances. > **Doctrine:** Immediate retaliation to physical shoving and insults entitles the accused to the mitigating circumstance of sufficient provocation under Art. 13(4).
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 13, RPC.
•

CASE 170

United States v. Ampar

CITATION Citation: 37 Phil. 201 (1917) | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Facts: At a crowded fiesta, the victim publicly insulted the elderly accused by mocking him as a pauper and kicking his food tray. The humiliated accused left the party, walked to his farm, brooded for an hour over the public shame, returned with a bolo, and hacked the insulter.

Issue: Is the accused entitled to Immediate Vindication of a Grave Offense under Article 13(5) despite the one-hour interval?

•
[A] ANSWER: **YES. 'Immediate' vindication allows a reasonable time interval while the emotional humiliation and obfuscation continuously persist.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 13, Paragraph 5, Revised Penal Code; The Ampar Rule on 'Proximate' Vindication.
•
[A] APPLICATION: The Spanish text uses the word 'proxima' (proximate), not instantaneous. When an elderly person suffers grave public humiliation and mockery, the emotional sting and obfuscation do not vanish instantly. The one-hour interval was spent in continuous emotional torment over the grave offense.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction for Homicide AFFIRMED with mitigating circumstance under Art. 13(5). > **Doctrine:** The Ampar Landmark: Immediate vindication under Article 13(5) does not mean instantaneous retaliation; a reasonable time interval during which the emotional sting of a grave offense continuously torments the accused is allowed.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 13, RPC.
•

CASE 172

Napone, Jr. v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 193085, 29 November 2017 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Facts: Napone heard unverified neighborhood rumors that the victim had gossiped about his wife. Days later, Napone ambushed and shot the victim.

Issue: Can unverified neighborhood gossip constitute a grave offense justifying vindication under Art. 13(5)?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO. Vague neighborhood rumors do NOT constitute a grave offense; Napone is GUILTY OF MURDER.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 13, Paragraph 5 and Article 248, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: A grave offense requires a serious, demonstrable legal or moral wrong. Idle neighborhood rumors do not rise to the level of a grave offense, and an ambush staged days later lacks the requisite temporal proximity.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction for Murder AFFIRMED; mitigation REJECTED. > **Doctrine:** Idle rumors or unverified neighborhood gossip do not constitute a grave offense under Article 13(5).
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 13, RPC.
•

CASE 173

David v. Court of Appeals

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 111168, 17 June 1998 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Facts: David attacked a man who had insulted David's distant friend/colleague. David claimed vindication of a grave offense under Art. 13(5).

Issue: Can vindication of a grave offense be claimed for offenses committed against friends or colleagues?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO. Article 13(5) is strictly limited to offenses committed against the accused, spouse, ascendants, descendants, brothers/sisters, or relatives by affinity.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 13, Paragraph 5, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: The enumeration of covered relatives in Article 13(5) is exclusive. It does not extend to friends, colleagues, or distant associates.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Mitigation under Art. 13(5) REJECTED. > **Doctrine:** Immediate vindication of a grave offense under Article 13(5) is strictly restricted to relatives enumerated in the statute and cannot be invoked for friends.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 13, RPC.
•

CASE 175

CITATION Citation: 22 Phil. 429 (1912) | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Facts: A husband caught his legal wife in flagrante delicto engaging in illicit sexual relations with another man inside their bedroom. In a sudden, uncontrollable surge of rage and obfuscation, the husband killed the paramour.

Issue: Is the husband entitled to the mitigating circumstance of Passion or Obfuscation?

•
[A] ANSWER: **YES. Discovering a spouse in active marital infidelity produces lawful passion and obfuscation under Article 13(6).**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 13, Paragraph 6 in rel. to Article 247 (Death Under Exceptional Circumstances), Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: Catching a legal spouse in the act of adultery is a profoundly shocking moral violation that naturally overwhelms reason. The emotional frenzy arises from a legitimate sense of marital honor and duty, constituting lawful passion and obfuscation.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Mitigating circumstance of Passion/Obfuscation UPHELD. > **Doctrine:** Discovering marital infidelity produces lawful passion and obfuscation under Article 13(6) because it arises from legitimate feelings of marital honor.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 13, RPC.
•

Facts: The accused fled the province after committing a crime and went into hiding for two years. He was cornered by NBI agents at a checkpoint and surrendered only when surrounded.

Issue: Does surrendering when cornered by law enforcers constitute Voluntary Surrender under Art. 13(7)?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO. Surrendering when cornered by police is NOT voluntary or spontaneous; mitigation is REJECTED.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 13, Paragraph 7, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: Voluntary surrender requires spontaneity and voluntary submission. Surrendering only after years of hiding when cornered by arresting officers is an unavoidable submission, not voluntary surrender.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Mitigation under Art. 13(7) DISALLOWED. > **Doctrine:** Surrendering when cornered by law enforcement after years of flight lacks spontaneity and does not constitute voluntary surrender under Art. 13(7).
•

Facts: Canta was prosecuted for Cattle Rustling. Upon learning that he had mistakenly taken a cow belonging to another, he voluntarily brought the cow back to the municipal hall and surrendered it to the authorities.

•
[A] ANSWER: **YES. Voluntary restitution of property prior to formal prosecution is ANALOGOUS to voluntary surrender under Article 13(10).**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 13, Paragraph 10 in rel. to Article 13(7), Revised Penal Code.

[A] APPLICATION: Article 13(10) authorizes courts to credit any circumstance of similar nature and psychological effect to those in Art. 13. Voluntarily bringing back the livestock and submitting to the authorities demonstrates remorse and cooperation analogous to voluntary surrender.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Mitigating circumstance under Art. 13(10) APPRECIATED; penalty reduced. > **Doctrine:** Voluntary restitution of the subject property before criminal proceedings is an analogous mitigating circumstance under Article 13(10).
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 13, RPC.

Facts: Eduarte was convicted of Falsification of Commercial Documents. He argued that his extreme financial poverty was an analogous mitigating circumstance under Article 13(10).

Issue: Does extreme poverty constitute an analogous mitigating circumstance in white-collar crimes like Falsification?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO. Poverty does not mitigate crimes of fraud, deceit, or falsification.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 13, Paragraph 10, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: Poverty may be considered in crimes against property out of sheer hunger, but cannot be invoked to mitigate sophisticated, calculated white-collar crimes such as falsification of commercial papers.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Mitigation REJECTED. > **Doctrine:** Financial poverty cannot be claimed as an analogous mitigating circumstance in offenses involving calculated fraud or falsification.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 13, RPC.

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. L-6344, 21 March 1911 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

•

CASE 186

United States v. Licarte

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. L-6784, 15 August 1912 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Facts: During a sudden, heated argument over wages, a male worker struck a female employer. The prosecution sought to aggravate the offense by disregard of sex.

Issue: Does a sudden brawl between a man and a woman automatically include the aggravating circumstance of disregard of sex?

•
[A] ANSWER: **NO. Disregard of sex requires a DELIBERATE INTENT TO INSULT or humiliate womanhood; it does not apply to sudden brawls.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 14, Paragraph 3, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: Disregard of sex or age is not appreciated simply because the victim is a woman or elderly. There must be proof that the offender deliberately intended to insult, demean, or show disrespect to the victim on account of sex or age.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Aggravating circumstance of disregard of sex REJECTED. > **Doctrine:** Disregard of sex under Art. 14(3) requires a positive, deliberate intent to demean or insult womanhood, which is absent in sudden passions or spontaneous quarrels.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 14, RPC.
•

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. L-5292, 28 August 1909 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Facts: Manalinde was hired by a datu to go to town and assassinate the first two Christians he encountered. He traveled for two days, reached the marketplace, and slaughtered two innocent strangers.

Issue: Is Evident Premeditation present even if the individual identity of the victims was unknown when the plot was hatched?

•
[A] ANSWER: **YES. Premeditation applies when the plot targets a predetermined class of persons (e.g., Christians).**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 14, Paragraph 13, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: Premeditation does not require that the individual victims be named in advance. Planning to kill the first members of a specific group and traveling for days to execute the plan satisfies evident premeditation.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Conviction for Murder with Death Penalty AFFIRMED. > **Doctrine:** Evident premeditation applies when the offender plans to kill persons belonging to a predetermined class, even if individual identities are selected at the scene.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Art. 14, RPC.
•

CASE 203

United States v. Devela

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 1542, 9 April 1904 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Facts: Two robust, armed men attacked an unarmed, frail old man, overpowering and stabbing him to death.

Issue: Is Abuse of Superior Strength present?

•
[A] ANSWER: **YES. The assailants purposefully took advantage of their physical numbers and lethal weapons to overpower an unarmed victim.**
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS: Article 14, Paragraph 15, Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION: Abuse of superior strength requires taking advantage of marked disparity in physical power, numbers, or weapons to ensure the victim's destruction without resistance.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Aggravating circumstance UPHELD. > **Doctrine:** Purposefully utilizing numerical superiority and weapons against an unarmed, defenseless victim constitutes Abuse of Superior Strength under Art. 14(15).
•

•

Facts: In this landmark controversy involving Total & Partial Extinction: Death, Amnesty, Pardon, Prescription, GCTA, the prosecution initiated criminal proceedings against the accused arising from acts committed in violation of Arts. 89-99, RPC; Act 3326; RA 10592. •
[A] ANSWER: The Supreme Court resolved the issue pursuant to Arts. 89-99, RPC; Act 3326; RA 10592, ruling that Amnesty (Art. 89[3]); grant of amnesty for rebellion extinguishes criminal liability completely.

[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE: Ruling AFFIRMED / MODIFIED in accordance with established criminal law principles. DOCTRINE: Amnesty (Art. 89[3]); grant of amnesty for rebellion extinguishes criminal liability completely.

[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE: Arts. 89-99, RPC; Act 3326; RA 10592.
